content:
The image shows a cross-section or split corn stalk. Key features:

- **Affected part**: Stalk (internal tissue visible)
- **Color**: The stalk exterior is tan/golden-brown (dried), with internal pith that appears **white/bleached** and shredded
- **Texture**: The internal pith is disintegrated, leaving hollow, stringy, fibrous vascular bundles — the pith has been completely consumed/degraded
- **Pattern**: The cortex (outer rind) is intact but the internal pith is collapsed and white-colored

This pattern — complete internal pith degradation leaving behind only vascular bundles, with white/light-colored internal discoloration — is characteristic of **Charcoal Stalk Rot** (*Macrophomina phaseolina*), which shreds the pith and leaves it gray-white with tiny black sclerotia, OR **Diplodia Stalk Rot**, which also causes internal pith rotting with a white/tan bleached appearance and shredded vascular tissue.

The white, bleached pith that is completely disintegrated (not gray with visible sclerotia) strongly points to **Charcoal Stalk Rot** — but the absence of visible black sclerotia and the clean white color also fits **Diplodia Stalk Rot**, which turns the pith white and causes complete disintegration of internal tissue leaving fibrous strands.

Diplodia stalk rot is associated with white/light internal pith rot and shredded vascular bundles exactly as shown. Charcoal rot typically shows grayish pith with scattered black sclerotia. The clean white color here favors Diplodia.
